report.source_text: After discontinuing antihistamines for 1 week, a water provocation test was administered. This involved regional contact using a damp cloth on the patient’s trunk, maintained at 35°C (figure 1A). After 20 min, there was a development of urticarial eruption on the trunk, which was consistent with the patient’s natural exposure to water (figure 1B).

report.source_text: At the 8-month follow-up, she did not report any further episodes of symptoms, unless a dosage of cetirizine was missed.

clinician.trajectory_summary: Adolescent female presented with 2-year history of immediate-onset pinpoint wheals with erythematous flares after water exposure of any temperature or source (showering, bathing, swimming, seawater, rain), lasting 30-60 minutes with spontaneous resolution, associated with abdominal discomfort when drinking water and reactions to animal saliva. On evaluation, physical examination revealed clear skin with absence of dermographism (E001). Laboratory workup including CBC, liver/renal function, urine analysis, immunoglobulins, and thyroid function tests was within normal limits, ruling out underlying systemic abnormalities (E002). Diagnostic confirmation was achieved via water provocation test using a damp cloth at 35°C for 20 minutes, which reproduced the urticarial eruption consistent with natural exposure (E003). Treatment was initiated with cetirizine 10mg daily, resulting in substantial symptom relief and discontinuation of prior montelukast therapy (E005). At 8-month follow-up, the patient remained symptom-free except when doses were missed (E006).
